title: Competitive Strategy
summary: How experienced debaters plan a round: off-case arguments in policy, choosing what to go for, managing time and prep, adapting to judges, and the terms you'll hear on the national circuit.

p: Besides answering the affirmative's case directly ("on-case"), negative teams in policy debate bring their own positions ("off-case"):
list: **Disadvantage (DA)**: the plan causes a harm. It needs **uniqueness** (the harm isn't happening now), a **link** (the plan causes it), and an **impact** (why it's bad). Affirmatives answer with non-unique, no link, link turn, and impact defense.
**Counterplan (CP)**: a different way to solve the problem without the disadvantage. It must be a reason to reject the plan, usually by being **competitive** (you can't or shouldn't do both).

**Topicality (T)**: the plan doesn't meet the resolution's words. The negative offers an interpretation, explains how the plan violates it, and gives reasons ("standards") why their reading is better for fair debate.

**Kritik (K)**: an argument that questions the assumptions or language of the other side's case, often drawing on philosophy or social theory. Some judges welcome these; others prefer arguments about the plan's results. Read the paradigm.
**Theory**: arguments about what debaters should be allowed to do (for example, whether a certain kind of counterplan is fair).

p: Early speeches put many arguments on the table; the last speeches should not. In the final rebuttal, **collapse**: choose the one or two arguments you're winning most clearly and that matter most, extend them fully, and weigh. A 2NR that goes for everything usually goes for nothing.
Ask: Which arguments did the other side answer weakly or drop? Which have the biggest impacts? Which will this judge understand and accept?

list: **Allocate time** before a rebuttal: write "1:30 on their case, 2:00 on ours, 0:30 weighing" at the top of your flow.
**Save prep** for the speeches that need it most, usually the last rebuttals.
**Prepare blocks**: written answers to common arguments, so you spend prep adapting rather than writing from scratch.
**Use cross-ex time** to think about your next speech when your partner is questioning.
**Speed** depends on the judge. Many national-circuit judges accept fast delivery; most local, state and homeschool judges don't. Clarity always wins over volume.
**Jargon**: say "they never answered our second argument" to a lay judge, not "they conceded C2, extend."
**Panels**: in front of mixed judges, explain as if to the least experienced and organize as if for the most.

p: On some circuits, teams share what cases they've run (called **disclosure**), so others can prepare. Whether or not your circuit does, keep notes on the arguments you meet at each tournament, and write answers before the next one. The best preparation is still to know both sides of the topic deeply, which the [topic pages](/debate/topics/) can help you start.

The same format can look very different on different circuits. National-circuit rounds can be fast and technical; local and state leagues often expect slower, persuasive speaking; homeschool leagues emphasize communication to a community judge. None is the "real" debate. Learn the expectations where you compete, and be ready to adapt when you travel.

practice: Write a disadvantage on a policy topic with uniqueness, link and impact, then write four affirmative answers to it.
Take your flow from your last round and write the final rebuttal you wish you'd given, collapsing to one argument.
Time yourself giving the same rebuttal for a lay judge and for a flow judge. What changed?
